vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: weaker than before, because you have not used it
a stage where progress stops for a while
something so familiar you no longer think about it
the situations where you feel safe and do not try hard
speaking smoothly, without building each sentence first
to use the familiar, safe option when the new one feels risky
a fixed point you measure later progress against

paras: He reads The Economist before breakfast, listens to three podcasts a week and finishes two or three novels a year, all in English. Ask him about a clause in a supply contract and he will find the problem before you have finished the sentence. Then put him on a call with a client in London, and something strange happens: the man who understands everything starts to speak in short, careful sentences, the same four or five structures over and over, and he leaves the call knowing that he said less than he thought. Language teachers have a name for this. It is not a lack of vocabulary, and it is not a limit. It is the advanced plateau, and it is the most common place for an intelligent adult learner to stop.

The plateau has a simple cause. Reading and listening are receptive: the sentence arrives already built, and your job is to recognize it. Speaking is productive: you have to build the sentence yourself, in real time, while somebody waits. A learner who reads every day develops an enormous receptive range and a productive range that is a fraction of it. Under pressure, he falls back on what is safe. The past perfect, the conditional, the reported question are all perfectly familiar on the page, but they never leave it, because in the moment the simple version is always available and never wrong enough to matter.

What moves a learner off the plateau is not more input. It is a benchmark and a small, deliberate risk. The benchmark shows him, in his own voice, how narrow his range really is; the risk is to use one structure he is not sure of in every conversation, and to accept the mistakes that come with it. Fluency usually improves first, because the pauses shrink before the errors do. Accuracy follows, often months later. The learners who never move are not the ones who make mistakes. They are the ones who have found a comfort zone so comfortable that nobody, including them, has noticed they are standing still.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: Since the first lesson, I have stopped translating everything in my head.
The structure that I still avoid is the reported question.
Although my reading is strong, my speaking has been slower to change.
If I recorded myself every month, I would hear the difference.
By the time I noticed the plateau, I had been on it for about a year.
It is a milestone, isn't it? But it is not the finish line.

listenings.text: The learners I worry about least are the ones who come to me and say they have stopped improving. That sentence tells me they are paying attention. The plateau is visible to them, which means we can work on it. The ones I worry about are the ones who have not noticed. Here is what I see, again and again, with advanced learners. They understand almost everything. Their reading is excellent. But under pressure, in a meeting or on a call, they fall back on the three or four structures they trust, and the other twenty never leave the page. So I ask them for one thing, and only one. In every conversation, use one structure you are not completely sure of. Just one. It will cost you a few mistakes. That is the price of leaving your comfort zone, and in my experience it is the only price that has ever bought anybody any progress.

I am not a native speaker, and I have worked in English for most of my career, so I have had to find a way to measure it. What I do is simple. Once a month I record five minutes of myself talking about my week. Always the same topic, always without notes, always five minutes. Then I wait. You should never listen to the new recording on the same day, because on the same day you hear what you meant to say. A week later you hear what you actually said, and that is a very different thing. When I started, the first change was fluency. Fewer pauses, fewer restarts, less time looking for the beginning of a sentence. Accuracy followed about six months later, and it followed almost by itself, because once you stop fighting for every sentence, you have the attention left over to get it right.
